title: Profinite change of components of a w-local affine ring
statement: Let $C$ be a commutative ring with w-local spectrum [def-weil-pbc-w-local], and write $P=\pi_0(\operatorname{Spec}C)$ for the quotient space of connected components. Then $P$ is profinite (compact Hausdorff totally disconnected), and the map from the closed point set of $\operatorname{Spec}C$ to $P$ is a homeomorphism. For every profinite space $T$ and continuous map $u:T\to P$, there exist a commutative $C$-algebra $D$ and a homeomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}D\cong\operatorname{Spec}C\times_P T$ over $\operatorname{Spec}C$, with $\pi_0(\operatorname{Spec}D)\cong T$ over $P$. The map $C\to D$ is ind-Zariski and ind-etale [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]. For every prime $\mathfrak q$ of $D$, the induced map $C_{\mathfrak q\cap C}\to D_{\mathfrak q}$ is an isomorphism. The spectrum of $D$ is w-local; its closed point set is the inverse image of the closed point set of $\operatorname{Spec}C$ and maps homeomorphically onto $T$. If $u$ is surjective, $\operatorname{Spec}D\to\operatorname{Spec}C$ is surjective.

proof.text: Put $X=\operatorname{Spec}C$ and $X^c$ equal to its closed point set. By [lem-weil-pbc-affine-scheme-qcqs], the affine scheme $X$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, so [lem-weil-pbc-qcqs-scheme-spectral] makes $X$ spectral. By [lem-weil-pbc-quasicompact-components-clopen-intersection], different components are separated by a clopen subset of $X$. A clopen subset is a union of components, since a connected component cannot meet both sides of a clopen separation; its image in the quotient $P$ is therefore clopen by the definition of the quotient topology. These images separate different points of $P$, proving Hausdorffness and total disconnectedness. Every cover of $P$ pulls back to a cover of the quasi-compact $X$, proving compactness. By the w-local hypothesis [def-weil-pbc-w-local], $X^c\to P$ is bijective. Its domain is closed in the quasi-compact $X$, hence quasi-compact by restricting an open cover and adjoining $X\setminus X^c$; quasi-compactness of $X$ is clause (iii) of [lem-weil-pbc-spec-basic-opens-unit-ideal-quasi-compact]. It is continuous, so a closed subset of $X^c$ has compact, hence closed, image in the Hausdorff $P$. Thus this continuous bijection is a homeomorphism. Denote its inverse by $s:P\to X^c$.

proof.text: Form the actual ring $A=\operatorname{LC}(T,C)$ of locally constant functions with pointwise operations and coefficient map given by constant functions. Use [lem-weil-pbc-locally-constant-prime-spectrum] to identify $\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $T\times X$ by $(t,\mathfrak p)\mapsto\{h:h(t)\in\mathfrak p\}$. Under this identification the coefficient spectrum map is the second projection, because the inverse image of this prime under the constant-function map is exactly $\mathfrak p$.

proof.text: Inside $T\times X$ take $E=\{(t,x):u(t)=\pi(x)\}$. It is closed: it is the inverse image of the closed diagonal of the Hausdorff $P$ under the continuous map $(t,x)\mapsto(u(t),\pi(x))$. It is a union of whole connected components. Indeed the first projection of any connected subset is a singleton in the totally disconnected $T$, and its second projection lies in a single component of $X$; therefore the defining equality is constant on each component of $T\times X$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-closed-component-spectrum-restriction] to this closed component union in $\operatorname{Spec}A$. Obtain a surjection $A\to D$ identifying $\operatorname{Spec}D$ homeomorphically with $E$ and identifying all local rings. Give $D$ its $C$-algebra structure through constant functions $C\to A\to D$. The preceding computation of the coefficient spectrum map shows this homeomorphism is over $X$, so it realizes the required topological pullback.

proof.text: The projection $E\to T$ is surjective because every component of $X$ contains its closed point $s(u(t))$. Its fibre over $t$ is homeomorphic to the nonempty connected component $\pi^{-1}(u(t))$ of $X$. Conversely every connected subset of $E$ maps to a singleton in $T$. Thus these fibres are exactly the connected components of $E$. The quotient topology gives a continuous bijection $\pi_0(\operatorname{Spec}D)\to T$. Its domain is quasi-compact: an open cover pulls back along the surjective quotient map to an open cover of the affine spectrum; clause (iii) of [lem-weil-pbc-spec-basic-opens-unit-ideal-quasi-compact] gives a finite subcover, and surjectivity gives a finite subcover downstairs. For a closed subset $F$ of this quotient, an open cover of $F$ together with its open complement covers the quotient, so $F$ is quasi-compact. Its continuous image in the Hausdorff $T$ is therefore compact and closed. The bijection is consequently closed, hence its inverse is continuous and it is a homeomorphism. The equality $u(t)=\pi(x)$ proves compatibility over $P$.

proof.text: Because $E$ is closed in $T\times X$, a singleton in $E$ is closed if and only if it is closed in $T\times X$. Since $T$ is Hausdorff, the latter holds for $(t,x)$ exactly when $x$ is closed in $X$: one direction uses the product of the two closed singletons, the other restricts to the closed slice $\{t\}\times X\cong X$. Hence the closed point set of $E$ is exactly the inverse image of $X^c$. It is closed, and is the graph $\{(t,s(u(t))):t\in T\}$, homeomorphic to $T$ with inverse $t\mapsto(t,s(u(t)))$. Each connected component computed in step 4 contains exactly this one closed point. These are precisely the two conditions in [def-weil-pbc-w-local], so $\operatorname{Spec}D$ is w-local.

proof.text: For $q\in\operatorname{Spec}D$ corresponding to $(t,\mathfrak p)\in E$, its inverse image in $A$ is $Q=\{h:h(t)\in\mathfrak p\}$, and its inverse image in $C$ is $\mathfrak p$. Evaluation at $t$ induces $A_Q\to C_{\mathfrak p}$, since a denominator outside $Q$ evaluates outside $\mathfrak p$; constant functions induce the reverse map. For any $h\in A$, the level set $N=\{z:h(z)=h(t)\}$ is clopen and contains $t$. Its characteristic function $e_N\in A$ is idempotent, lies outside $Q$, and satisfies $e_Nh=e_N\operatorname{const}(h(t))$. In $A_Q$ it is an invertible idempotent, hence equals $1$, giving $h=\operatorname{const}(h(t))$. Applying this also to denominators proves the two maps are inverse on every fraction. Now compose $C_{\mathfrak p}\cong A_Q$ with $A_Q\cong D_q$ from [lem-weil-pbc-closed-component-spectrum-restriction]. The composite sends $c/a$ to its image in $D$ divided by the image of $a$, so is exactly the induced local-ring map of $C\to D$, rather than merely an abstract isomorphism.

proof.text: The map $C\to D$ identifies all local rings by step 6 and has w-local target by step 5. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-local-rings-ind-zariski] with $A=C$, $B=D$. It gives precisely a filtered colimit presentation by finite products of principal localizations of $C$, which is the stronger ind-Zariski meaning in [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]. In that definition such a presentation is an ind-etale presentation as well, giving the ind-etale assertion. This also explains why merely citing the weaker Stacks definition of ind-Zariski would not have sufficed.

proof.text: If $u$ is surjective and $x\in X$, choose $t\in T$ with $u(t)=\pi(x)$. Then $(t,x)\in E$, and its corresponding point of $\operatorname{Spec}D$ maps to $x$. This proves surjectivity of the coefficient spectrum map, including the vacuous empty-spectrum case.
